strengths: The motivating SCM provides a clear, analytically checkable example showing why both contextual information and the choice of intervention variables can matter.

Combining POMPS reduction with contextual GP optimisation and an average-UCB scope-selection rule is a useful algorithmic direction. Separating scope-selection regret from action-selection regret provides a helpful analytical framework.

The controlled experiments use 110 seeds, 700 interventions, uncertainty intervals, and a common optimisation backend. Context, noise, and backend ablations provide useful supporting evidence, and the manuscript acknowledges a setting where CoBO converges faster.
weaknesses: The reduction from general mixed policies to Algorithm 2 is not justified. Definition 1 permits a sequential scope {(X1;∅),(X2;C)} with X1→C: C depends on an earlier intervention and cannot be observed before jointly choosing both actions. Sections 3 and B.1 instead assume fixed, intervention-independent context distributions and replace scopes with unions of action/context variables. Additional restrictions or a sequential optimisation treatment are needed to establish feasibility and guarantees for the stated causal setting.

Theorem 1 has substantive proof gaps. On page 27, the action loss f_i*(c)−f_i(x,c) is bounded by the range of f_i* across contexts. This inequality is false when the optimal value is constant across contexts but actions have different rewards. Also, Equation (21) and the concluding proof bound use c(T), defined through worst-arm information gain γ(T), whereas Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 claim the stronger arm-averaged information gain dependence. That improvement is not derived. These issues require correction before the stated guarantees can be accepted.

The theoretical and experimental algorithms are insufficiently connected. The guarantees assume known GP kernels, independent GP functions, Gaussian observation noise, and exact UCB maximisation; the experiments use HEBO with learned transformations and SCM-generated rewards. The manuscript does not establish that this implementation inherits the guarantees. Decreasing average regret over 700 iterations also does not establish an asymptotic sublinear rate.

The evaluation covers a few hand-designed SCMs, including a synthetic medical example. CaBO and CoBO are useful diagnostic comparisons, but Functional Causal BO is a particularly relevant missing baseline. There is also no comparison against simpler scope-selection schedules that isolates the contribution of the proposed average-UCB index. The existing ablations address context and optimisation backends, rather than this central algorithmic choice.

The scalability claims exceed the evidence. Section 3 explicitly retains exponential brute-force POMPS enumeration. Appendix A.3 adds many redundant variables while retaining only two candidate scopes, demonstrating dimensionality reduction but not scalability to many competing scopes. Preprocessing costs, end-to-end runtimes, and scaling with the number of candidate scopes are not reported.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the supplied PDF claims a public implementation but provides no repository link or concrete exploration schedules and optimisation settings. Experimental definitions also contain consequential inconsistencies: Appendix A.1.2 substitutes Cancer into a PSA equation that does not contain Cancer, and Appendix A.3 defines C4 through itself. These equations need correction to make the environments and reported optima unambiguous.
